evidence.title: Roles of Sulfites in Reverse Osmosis (RO) Plants and Adverse Effects in RO Operation.
evidence.abstract: More than 60 years have passed since UCLA first announced the development of an innovative asymmetric cellulose acetate reverse osmosis (RO) membrane in 1960. This innovation opened a gate to use RO for commercial use. RO is now ubiquitous in water treatment and has been used for various applications, including seawater desalination, municipal water treatment, wastewater reuse, ultra-pure water (UPW) production, and industrial process waters, etc. RO is a highly integrated system consisting of a series of unit processes: (1) intake system, (2) pretreatment, (3) RO system, (4) post-treatment, and (5) effluent treatment and discharge system. In each step, a variety of chemicals are used. Among those, sulfites (sodium bisulfite and sodium metabisulfite) have played significant roles in RO, such as dechlorination, preservatives, shock treatment, and sanitization, etc. Sulfites especially became necessary as dechlorinating agents because polyamide hollow-fiber and aromatic thin-film composite RO membranes developed in the late 1960s and 1970s were less tolerable with residual chlorine. In this review, key applications of sulfites are explained in detail. Furthermore, as it is reported that sulfites have some adverse effects on RO membranes and processes, such phenomena will be clarified. In particular, the following two are significant concerns using sulfites: RO membrane oxidation catalyzed by heavy metals and a trigger of biofouling. This review sheds light on the mechanism of membrane oxidation and triggering biofouling by sulfites. Some countermeasures are also introduced to alleviate such problems.

evidence.title: Progress and Prospects of Nanocellulose-Based Membranes for Desalination and Water Treatment.
evidence.abstract: Membrane-based desalination has proved to be the best solution for solving the water shortage issues globally. Membranes are extremely beneficial in the effective recovery of clean water from contaminated water sources, however, the durability as well as the separation efficiency of the membranes are restricted by the type of membrane materials/additives used in the preparation processes. Nanocellulose is one of the most promising green materials for nanocomposite preparation due to its biodegradability, renewability, abundance, easy modification, and exceptional mechanical properties. This nanocellulose has been used in membrane development for desalination application in the recent past. The study discusses the application of membranes based on different nanocellulose forms such as cellulose nanocrystals, cellulose nanofibrils, and bacterial nanocellulose for water desalination applications such as nanofiltration, reverse osmosis, pervaporation, forward osmosis, and membrane distillation. From the analysis of studies, it was confirmed that the nanocellulose-based membranes are effective in the desalination application. The chemical modification of nanocellulose can definitely improve the surface affinity as well as the reactivity of membranes for the efficient separation of specific contaminants/ions.

evidence.title: Coverage-Aware Break-Even Conditions for Polymeric Membrane-Based Water Reuse in Arid Urban Systems.
evidence.abstract: A utility reclaiming effluent with polymeric membranes must choose a configuration and a deployment coverage. A coverage-aware volume and cost model for an illustrative arid zone of 10Mm3/yr compares ultrafiltration (Configuration A) with ultrafiltration plus polyamide thin-film-composite reverse osmosis (Configuration B). Membrane parameters are literature-derived, eligibility and placement assumed, and no experiments were performed. At 50% coverage and 1 USD/m 3 , Configuration A avoids 11.5 percentage points of potable input at 0.48 USD/m 3 and Configuration B 20.4 points at 0.70 USD/m 3 , or 0.56 and 0.82 USD/m 3 without real-loss credit. Break-even coverages are 11.7% and 11.5%. Configuration B is preferable above a crossover value of 0.98 USD/m 3 (1.15 without loss credit) and leads in 46.2% of paired draws at 1 USD/m 3 . Feed salinity, regulation, concentrate cost, and capital and financing costs move the crossover most. Under independent inputs and assumed eligibility, approved demand rather than recovery limits volume in at least 98.8% of draws, and placement dominates net-benefit variance. Adverse feed conditions that couple operating and cost parameters make treatment costs comparably influential for Configuration B. The thresholds are conditional criteria, not city-specific predictions.

evidence.title: Advances and Challenges in Aerobic Granular Sludge Membrane Bioreactors for Treating Sulfamethoxazole in Wastewater.
evidence.abstract: Sulfamethoxazole (SMX) is one of the most frequently detected antibiotics in aquatic environments and is difficult to remove by conventional biological treatment because of its persistence, potential toxicity to microbial communities, and associated risk of antibiotic resistance selection. Aerobic granular sludge membrane bioreactors (AGMBRs), which combine the compact and stratified structure of aerobic granular sludge with membrane-based solid-liquid separation, have emerged as a promising platform for SMX-contaminated wastewater treatment because they provide high biomass retention, decoupled sludge retention time (SRT) and hydraulic retention time (HRT), and stable effluent quality. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in AGMBRs for SMX removal, with emphasis on how operating parameters (e.g., dissolved oxygen, hydraulic retention time, organic loading rate, C/N ratio, and sludge retention time) and membrane-related factors (e.g., membrane flux, aeration-induced shear, membrane type, and pore size) affect treatment performance and process stability. The main SMX attenuation pathways in AGMBRs are discussed from three perspectives: sorption and partitioning within granules and extracellular polymeric substances (EPSs), microbial biodegradation and co-metabolism, and membrane retention that prolongs effective contact time and shapes microbial ecology. Particular attention is given to the dual role of EPS and soluble microbial products (SMPs), which contribute to granule stability and SMX tolerance but also accelerate membrane fouling through cake-layer formation, pore blocking, and transmembrane pressure increase. Current challenges include incomplete understanding of transformation products, ARG- and MGE-related risks, long-term fouling-biodegradation interactions, and the lack of pilot-scale validation. Future research should therefore focus on mechanism clarification, integrated control of removal and fouling, energy-efficient operation, and scale-up of AGMBRs for practical antibiotic wastewater treatment.

evidence.title: Piezoelectric sterilization techniques: from innovations to applications.
evidence.abstract: Piezoelectric materials have emerged as promising non-thermal, chemical-free sterilization agents, offering clear advantages over traditional methods such as heat, UV, or disinfectants. Their antimicrobial activity arises from direct microbial membrane disruption and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation under mechanical stimuli like ultrasound or vibration via piezodynamic reactions. These approaches preserve material integrity, making them ideal for implants, wound dressings, and biofilm prevention. Recent advances focus on enhancing piezoelectricity via defect engineering, dopants, and band structure optimization to improve ROS production. This review highlights progress in piezoelectric materials as smart, sustainable antimicrobial platforms with broad biomedical and environmental applications.

evidence.title: When a Sensor Loses Its Oracle: Three-Arm Differential Observability and Zero-Oracle Fail-Closed Abstention for Membrane Fouling Diagnostics
evidence.abstract:
Soft sensors for reverse osmosis (RO) and forward osmosis (FO) desalination must separate reversible concentration polarization (CP) from irreversible mineral scaling and biofouling while remaining resilient to sensor drift, temperature shocks, and reference-channel contamination. We identify two structural vulnerabilities in differential membrane diagnostics: (1) a 2-arm differential cartridge cannot distinguish reference-arm contamination from test-arm cleanliness, producing a 71.17% estimation error without warning under 10% partial reference fouling (Scenario NC5), whereas a 3-arm differential manifold with a witness-ratio guard (τref = |rref(t) − rref,0|/rref,0 > 0.03) restores Rank-2 Fisher observability (det I > 0) and cuts error to 7.72%; and (2) autonomous diagnostic codebases suffer from oracle leakage when simulator ground-truth fields (ground_truth_scale_um) or synthetic nominal reference values remain accessible inside production classes or when invariants rely on strip-prone assert statements under python -O. After hardening CommercialPhysicalWitnessB (removing all simulator fields, enforcing explicit runtime ValueError guards across 19/19 standard and -O unit tests), the zero-oracle estimator achieves 5/5 (100%) clean operating-sweep coverage and reduces false-confident commits on 9 adversarial fault challenges from 7/9 (77.8%, SystemA) and 8/9 (88.9%, SystemC/R0) to 1/9 (11.1%, residual C07 80 nm sub-resolution CaSO4 film), while correctly abstaining (21/21 ABSTAIN_MISSING_REFERENCE_EVIDENCE) on 21 published literature rows that lack a physical reference channel.

Evidence classification: simulation only (SIMULATION_VERIFIED_WET_LAB_UNTESTED). No wet-lab membrane experiment has been executed; zero wet-lab membrane hours. Published as a methods protocol / registered-protocol preprint, not as experimental results. The \$551.32 COTS benchtop flow-loop protocol in Section 3 is pre-registered and specified, not run. All metrics are simulation replays and literature-row audits, deterministically reproduced by reproduce_paper2_zero_oracle_pareto.py, included in the reproducibility bundle. Reproducibility code in the bundle is Apache License 2.0; paper text is CC BY 4.0.

evidence.title: Water Treatment for "Green" Hydrogen Production in Alkaline Electrolyzers
evidence.abstract: This paper systematizes typical feedwater quality requirements for AWE systems and explains why the parameters of specific electrical resistance (resistivity) and electrical conductivity are interrelated quality-control indicators. The main technological solutions for producing demineralized water are reviewed, including mechanical filtration, activated carbon filtration, reverse osmosis (RO), and electrodeionization (EDI). Key operational risks are also discussed, such as channeling, increased pressure drop (ΔP), carryover of carbon fines, biofouling, and oxidative damage to RO membranes. As a practical example, an aggregated process scheme is presented for a water treatment line designed to produce demineralized (DM) water with a target quality of approximately 1 MΩ·cm or higher. Recommendations are provided for monitoring (conductivity/resistivity, SiO₂, TOC, Cl⁻, iron), filter backwash regimes, protection of RO membranes from chlorine, and reduction of factors that contribute to increased cell voltage during AWE operation.

evidence.title: Plasma-Enhanced Magnetron Sputtering: A Novel Approach for Biofunctional Metal Nanoparticle Coatings on Reverse Osmosis Composite Membranes
evidence.abstract: Reverse osmosis (RO) is the most common method for treating salt and brackish water. As a membrane-driven process, a key challenge for RO systems is their susceptibility to scaling and biofouling. To address these issues, functional coatings utilizing metal nanoparticles (MNPs) are developed. In this study, silver, gold, and copper nanoparticles are applied onto thin-film composite (TFC) membranes using plasma-enhanced magnetron sputtering. The elemental composition, surface morphology, and hydrophilicity of the coatings are analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and contact angle measurements. The antimicrobial properties and the filtration efficiency of the coated membranes are assessed through application-specific experimental setups. Silver and copper nanoparticles exhibit superior antimicrobial properties, reducing microorganism adhesion by a factor of 103 compared to uncoated membranes. Under appropriate coating conditions, no deterioration in filtration performance is observed. Enhancing the adhesion of MNPs is necessary for achieving sustained release of metal ions.

evidence.title: Ideal Desalination through Graphyne-4 Membrane: Nanopores for Quantized Water Transport
evidence.abstract: Graphyne-4 sheet exhibits promising potential for nanoscale desalination to achieve both high water permeability and salt rejection rate. Extensive molecular dynamics simulations on pore-size effects suggest that graphyne-4, with 4 acetylene bonds between two adjacent phenyl rings, has the best performance with 100% salt rejection and an unprecedented water permeability, to our knowledge, of ~13L/cm2/day/MPa, about 10 times higher than the state-of-the-art nanoporous graphene reported previously (Nano Lett.s 2012, 12, 3602-3608). In addition, the membrane entails very low energy consumption for producing 1m3 of fresh water, i.e., 3.6e-3 kWh/m3, three orders of magnitude less than the prevailing commercial membranes based on reverse osmosis. Water flow rate across the graphyne-4 sheet exhibits intriguing nonlinear dependence on the pore size owing to the quantized nature of water flow at the nanoscale. Such novel transport behavior has important implications to the design of highly effective and efficient desalination membranes.

evidence.title: High-flux water desalination with interfacial salt sieving effect in nanoporous carbon composite membranes
evidence.abstract: Nanoporous carbon composite membranes, comprising a layer of porous carbon fiber structures with an average channel width of 30-60 nm grown on a porous ceramic substrate, are found to exhibit robust desalination effect with high freshwater flux. In three different membrane processes of vacuum membrane distillation, reverse osmosis and forward osmosis, the carbon composite membrane showed 100% salt rejection with 3.5 to 20 times higher freshwater flux compared to existing polymeric membranes. Thermal accounting experiments found that at least 80% of the freshwater pass through the carbon composite membrane with no phase change. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a unique salt rejection mechanism. When seawater is interfaced with either vapor or the surface of carbon, one to three interfacial atomic layers contain no salt ions. Below the liquid entry pressure, the salt solution is stopped at the openings to the porous channels and forms a meniscus, while the surface layer of freshwater can feed the surface diffusion flux that is fast-transported on the surfaces of the carbon fibers, driven by the chemical potential gradient. As the surface-transported water does not involve a phase change, hence that component involves no energy expenditure in the form of latent heat.

evidence.title: Mathematical modelling and numerical simulation of reverse-osmosis desalination
evidence.abstract: The reverse osmosis membrane module is an integral element of a desalination system as it determines the overall performance of the desalination plant. The fraction of clean water that can be recovered via this process is often limited by salt precipitation which plays a critical role in its sustainability. In this work, we present a model to study the complex interplay between flow, transport and precipitation processes in reverse osmosis membranes, which together influence recovery and in turn process sustainability. A reactive porous interface model describes the membrane with a dynamic evolving porosity and permeability to capture the scaling and clogging of the membrane. An open-source finite-volume numerical solver is implemented within the OpenFOAM library and numerical tests are presented here showing the effect of the various parameters of the model and the robustness of the model to describe a wide range of operating conditions.

evidence.title: Prediction, Diagnosis and Prevention of Fouling in Seawater Reverse Osmosis Membrane Systems.
evidence.abstract: The performance of pre-treatment and reverse osmosis (RO) membrane systems of a reverse osmosis (SWRO) desalination plant was evaluated using both in-situ fouling monitoring methods and theoretical standardisation and normalisation methods. The results showed that overall performance of the plant deteriorated after 6 months of operation due to fouling. In order to determine the identity and cause of th~ fouling two SWRO membranes were subjected to destructive membrane autopsy. The results showed formation of severe fouling on the surface of both membranes. Microscopic studies using atomic force microscopy (AFM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with Energy Dispersion X-ray spectrometer (EDX), elucidated this layer. AFM, SEM and EDX results showed different types of fouling includes scaling, colloidal and biological fouling. The presence of these foulants on the membrane surfaces indicates malfunctions in the pre-treatment systems used 'in the plant, ultimately resulting in the formation of composite fouling. The effect of this composite fouling on the performance of the RO membrane systems was investigated using a laboratory-scale RO unit and raw seawater samples from the Mediterranean and the North Seas. A rapid flux decline was observed. In order to eliminate the formation of the composite fouling in the RO membrane systems, a novel fouling prevention method was examined. This was a depth ~ filter (DisruptorTM) made of nanoalumina fibres upstream 'to the RO membranes. The results show that this depth filter removes the majority of substances which cause the fouling on the RO membranes. Results are discussed in relation to the practicalities, of desalination plant operation.

evidence.title: Assessing graphene oxide for water desalination applications
evidence.abstract: Water desalination plays a critical role in augmenting the fresh water supplies for water scarce regions. However, despite considerable improvements in system efficiencies, it still remains six to ten times more expensive than treating freshwater for drinking. As a result, the construction and operation of a desalination plant places considerable economic burden on the regions that require such an investment. As more and more regions experience water stress due to climate change, increased industrial consumption, and population growth, materials engineering will play a role in improving the economics. The membranes used in today's reverse osmosis plants are made from polymers that are fragile, limited in the flux, and typically operate at 70% of their rated performance due to biofouling. Following the exciting proposition of using graphene as a size-exclusion based desalination membrane, there has been a great deal of revived interest in the development of new membrane materials that overcome these challenges. Graphene oxide, made from the chemical exfoliation of graphite, has served as a promising candidate for membrane applications because it is cheaper than graphene to produce and yet demonstrates similar benefits of resilience and increased permeability. In this work, we take a critical look at three aspects of graphene oxide as it applies to the development of water desalination membranes. First, we present an atomic study of the structure of graphene oxide (GO) that is produced in bulk quantities. In contrast to previous work, which has examined particularly defect free GO, we find that GO develops a nanocrystalline structure in support of a Dynamic Structural Model in its hexagonal carbon lattice. Second, we detail the development of a new cross-linker that enables the fabrication of stable GO films with sub-nanometer interlayer spacing and demonstrated nanofiltration performance. The process of cross-linking and membrane fabrication is entirely solution based and therefore promising for scale up. Finally, we evaluate the techno-economic feasibility of a GO as a water desalination material with a comparison between estimated production cost and savings in terms of the levelized cost of water. evidence.title: Technological challenges of seawater desalination: analysis of future opportunities
evidence.abstract: This paper deals with an assessment of solar thermal-powered desalination technologies in order to identify key issues for developing market opportunities.The topic of selecting the best solar desalination solution is analysed, case by case, considering different scenes: i) Rural communities with limited fresh water demand; ii) Regions with high demands of both, water and electricity and iii) Intermediate water demands.Detailed analyses of solar thermal-driven desalination -i.e.distillation and Reverse Osmosis (RO) -in comparison to solar PV/RO are presented.The quantitative assessment performed highlights that membrane distillation systems, when fully developed, will have market opportunities at very small-capacity seawater desalination systems.Besides that, dish concentrators coupled to micro gas turbines in case of limited water demand is a promising option.A single unit could produce about 10 m3/h of fresh water from seawater and several units could be coupled to drive the same desalination plant.Moreover, the only stand-alone systems with market opportunities for intermediate water production are based on reverse osmosis driven by parabolic troughs or linear Fresnel concentrators by means of organic Rankine Cycles.Finally, water demands over 25,000 m 3 /d require both, a solar power plant and a reverse osmosis desalination plant.

evidence.title: Parameters affecting the desalination of seawater reverse osmosis : pre-treatments, membranes processes and environmental impact
evidence.abstract: Paramètres affectants le dessalement de l'eau de mer par osmose inverse : prétraitement, procédés membranaires et impact environnemental Ce travail a été réalisé dans le cadre d’une étude lancée par la compagnie HUTA sur ses installations de dessalement d’eau de mer. Le procédé de dessalement des eaux de mer le plus utilisé pour la production d’eau douce est l’osmose inverse (SWRO). Une station type, installée dans d’une zone industrielle, a été choisie pour mener cette étude d’optimisation du fonctionnement pour réduire les coûts d’exploitation. L’impact des rejets des rejets sur le milieu naturel a été également étudié. La station de dessalement sélectionnée pour les travaux de recherches est située dans la région Ouest de l’Arabie Saoudite à 160 km au nord de Djeddah, dans une zone industrielle pétrochimique (Raffinerie PETRO RABIGH), site ultra sécurisée, les captages des eaux de mer se font dans la zone côtière proche du site en Mer Rouge.L’étude se concentre principalement sur 3 parties : La première concerne la prise d’eau "INTAKE", différent mode captage ont été testé avec l’installation d’un ouvrage développé spécifiquement pour la station de Rabigh en s’adaptant aux règles imposées par les autorités Saoudienne. La deuxième est réservée aux procédés membranaires et l’importance des prétraitements dans la filière de désalinisation. La dernière partie concerne l’étude d’impact environnemental des rejets industriels "OUTLET" sur le milieu récepteur.

system.value: Progress and Prospects of Nanocellulose-Based Membranes for Desalination and Water Treatment.

abstract.value: Membrane-based desalination has proved to be the best solution for solving the water shortage issues globally. Membranes are extremely beneficial in the effective recovery of clean water from contaminated water sources, however, the durability as well as the separation efficiency of the membranes are restricted by the type of membrane materials/additives used in the preparation processes. Nanocellulose is one of the most promising green materials for nanocomposite preparation due to its biodegradability, renewability, abundance, easy modification, and exceptional mechanical properties. This nanocellulose has been used in membrane development for desalination application in the recent past. The study discusses the application of membranes based on different nanocellulose forms such as cellulose nanocrystals, cellulose nanofibrils, and bacterial nanocellulose for water desalination applications such as nanofiltration, reverse osmosis, pervaporation, forward osmosis, and membrane distillation. From the analysis of studies, it was confirmed that the nanocellulose-based membranes are effective in the desalination application. The chemical modification of nanocellulose can definitely improve the surface affinity as well as the reactivity of membranes for the efficient separation of specific contaminants/ions.

system.value: Coverage-Aware Break-Even Conditions for Polymeric Membrane-Based Water Reuse in Arid Urban Systems.

abstract.value: A utility reclaiming effluent with polymeric membranes must choose a configuration and a deployment coverage. A coverage-aware volume and cost model for an illustrative arid zone of 10Mm3/yr compares ultrafiltration (Configuration A) with ultrafiltration plus polyamide thin-film-composite reverse osmosis (Configuration B). Membrane parameters are literature-derived, eligibility and placement assumed, and no experiments were performed. At 50% coverage and 1 USD/m 3 , Configuration A avoids 11.5 percentage points of potable input at 0.48 USD/m 3 and Configuration B 20.4 points at 0.70 USD/m 3 , or 0.56 and 0.82 USD/m 3 without real-loss credit. Break-even coverages are 11.7% and 11.5%. Configuration B is preferable above a crossover value of 0.98 USD/m 3 (1.15 without loss credit) and leads in 46.2% of paired draws at 1 USD/m 3 . Feed salinity, regulation, concentrate cost, and capital and financing costs move the crossover most. Under independent inputs and assumed eligibility, approved demand rather than recovery limits volume in at least 98.8% of draws, and placement dominates net-benefit variance. Adverse feed conditions that couple operating and cost parameters make treatment costs comparably influential for Configuration B. The thresholds are conditional criteria, not city-specific predictions.

system.value: When a Sensor Loses Its Oracle: Three-Arm Differential Observability and Zero-Oracle Fail-Closed Abstention for Membrane Fouling Diagnostics

abstract.value:
Soft sensors for reverse osmosis (RO) and forward osmosis (FO) desalination must separate reversible concentration polarization (CP) from irreversible mineral scaling and biofouling while remaining resilient to sensor drift, temperature shocks, and reference-channel contamination. We identify two structural vulnerabilities in differential membrane diagnostics: (1) a 2-arm differential cartridge cannot distinguish reference-arm contamination from test-arm cleanliness, producing a 71.17% estimation error without warning under 10% partial reference fouling (Scenario NC5), whereas a 3-arm differential manifold with a witness-ratio guard (τref = |rref(t) − rref,0|/rref,0 > 0.03) restores Rank-2 Fisher observability (det I > 0) and cuts error to 7.72%; and (2) autonomous diagnostic codebases suffer from oracle leakage when simulator ground-truth fields (ground_truth_scale_um) or synthetic nominal reference values remain accessible inside production classes or when invariants rely on strip-prone assert statements under python -O. After hardening CommercialPhysicalWitnessB (removing all simulator fields, enforcing explicit runtime ValueError guards across 19/19 standard and -O unit tests), the zero-oracle estimator achieves 5/5 (100%) clean operating-sweep coverage and reduces false-confident commits on 9 adversarial fault challenges from 7/9 (77.8%, SystemA) and 8/9 (88.9%, SystemC/R0) to 1/9 (11.1%, residual C07 80 nm sub-resolution CaSO4 film), while correctly abstaining (21/21 ABSTAIN_MISSING_REFERENCE_EVIDENCE) on 21 published literature rows that lack a physical reference channel.

Evidence classification: simulation only (SIMULATION_VERIFIED_WET_LAB_UNTESTED). No wet-lab membrane experiment has been executed; zero wet-lab membrane hours. Published as a methods protocol / registered-protocol preprint, not as experimental results. The \$551.32 COTS benchtop flow-loop protocol in Section 3 is pre-registered and specified, not run. All metrics are simulation replays and literature-row audits, deterministically reproduced by reproduce_paper2_zero_oracle_pareto.py, included in the reproducibility bundle. Reproducibility code in the bundle is Apache License 2.0; paper text is CC BY 4.0.

system.value: Water Treatment for "Green" Hydrogen Production in Alkaline Electrolyzers

abstract.value: This paper systematizes typical feedwater quality requirements for AWE systems and explains why the parameters of specific electrical resistance (resistivity) and electrical conductivity are interrelated quality-control indicators. The main technological solutions for producing demineralized water are reviewed, including mechanical filtration, activated carbon filtration, reverse osmosis (RO), and electrodeionization (EDI). Key operational risks are also discussed, such as channeling, increased pressure drop (ΔP), carryover of carbon fines, biofouling, and oxidative damage to RO membranes. As a practical example, an aggregated process scheme is presented for a water treatment line designed to produce demineralized (DM) water with a target quality of approximately 1 MΩ·cm or higher. Recommendations are provided for monitoring (conductivity/resistivity, SiO₂, TOC, Cl⁻, iron), filter backwash regimes, protection of RO membranes from chlorine, and reduction of factors that contribute to increased cell voltage during AWE operation.

system.value: Plasma-Enhanced Magnetron Sputtering: A Novel Approach for Biofunctional Metal Nanoparticle Coatings on Reverse Osmosis Composite Membranes

abstract.value: Reverse osmosis (RO) is the most common method for treating salt and brackish water. As a membrane-driven process, a key challenge for RO systems is their susceptibility to scaling and biofouling. To address these issues, functional coatings utilizing metal nanoparticles (MNPs) are developed. In this study, silver, gold, and copper nanoparticles are applied onto thin-film composite (TFC) membranes using plasma-enhanced magnetron sputtering. The elemental composition, surface morphology, and hydrophilicity of the coatings are analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and contact angle measurements. The antimicrobial properties and the filtration efficiency of the coated membranes are assessed through application-specific experimental setups. Silver and copper nanoparticles exhibit superior antimicrobial properties, reducing microorganism adhesion by a factor of 103 compared to uncoated membranes. Under appropriate coating conditions, no deterioration in filtration performance is observed. Enhancing the adhesion of MNPs is necessary for achieving sustained release of metal ions.

system.value: Ideal Desalination through Graphyne-4 Membrane: Nanopores for Quantized Water Transport

abstract.value: Graphyne-4 sheet exhibits promising potential for nanoscale desalination to achieve both high water permeability and salt rejection rate. Extensive molecular dynamics simulations on pore-size effects suggest that graphyne-4, with 4 acetylene bonds between two adjacent phenyl rings, has the best performance with 100% salt rejection and an unprecedented water permeability, to our knowledge, of ~13L/cm2/day/MPa, about 10 times higher than the state-of-the-art nanoporous graphene reported previously (Nano Lett.s 2012, 12, 3602-3608). In addition, the membrane entails very low energy consumption for producing 1m3 of fresh water, i.e., 3.6e-3 kWh/m3, three orders of magnitude less than the prevailing commercial membranes based on reverse osmosis. Water flow rate across the graphyne-4 sheet exhibits intriguing nonlinear dependence on the pore size owing to the quantized nature of water flow at the nanoscale. Such novel transport behavior has important implications to the design of highly effective and efficient desalination membranes.

system.value: High-flux water desalination with interfacial salt sieving effect in nanoporous carbon composite membranes

abstract.value: Nanoporous carbon composite membranes, comprising a layer of porous carbon fiber structures with an average channel width of 30-60 nm grown on a porous ceramic substrate, are found to exhibit robust desalination effect with high freshwater flux. In three different membrane processes of vacuum membrane distillation, reverse osmosis and forward osmosis, the carbon composite membrane showed 100% salt rejection with 3.5 to 20 times higher freshwater flux compared to existing polymeric membranes. Thermal accounting experiments found that at least 80% of the freshwater pass through the carbon composite membrane with no phase change. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a unique salt rejection mechanism. When seawater is interfaced with either vapor or the surface of carbon, one to three interfacial atomic layers contain no salt ions. Below the liquid entry pressure, the salt solution is stopped at the openings to the porous channels and forms a meniscus, while the surface layer of freshwater can feed the surface diffusion flux that is fast-transported on the surfaces of the carbon fibers, driven by the chemical potential gradient. As the surface-transported water does not involve a phase change, hence that component involves no energy expenditure in the form of latent heat.

Thermal accounting experiments found that at least 80% of the freshwater pass through the carbon composite membrane with no phase change. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a unique salt rejection mechanism. When seawater is interfaced with either vapor or the surface of carbon, one to three interfacial atomic layers contain no salt ions. Below the liquid entry pressure, the salt solution is stopped at the openings to the porous channels and forms a meniscus, while the surface layer of freshwater can feed the surface diffusion flux that is fast-transported on the surfaces of the carbon fibers, driven by the chemical potential gradient. As the surface-transported water does not involve a phase change, hence that component involves no energy expenditure in the form of latent heat.

system.value: Mathematical modelling and numerical simulation of reverse-osmosis desalination

abstract.value: The reverse osmosis membrane module is an integral element of a desalination system as it determines the overall performance of the desalination plant. The fraction of clean water that can be recovered via this process is often limited by salt precipitation which plays a critical role in its sustainability. In this work, we present a model to study the complex interplay between flow, transport and precipitation processes in reverse osmosis membranes, which together influence recovery and in turn process sustainability. A reactive porous interface model describes the membrane with a dynamic evolving porosity and permeability to capture the scaling and clogging of the membrane. An open-source finite-volume numerical solver is implemented within the OpenFOAM library and numerical tests are presented here showing the effect of the various parameters of the model and the robustness of the model to describe a wide range of operating conditions.

system.value: Prediction, Diagnosis and Prevention of Fouling in Seawater Reverse Osmosis Membrane Systems.

abstract.value: The performance of pre-treatment and reverse osmosis (RO) membrane systems of a reverse osmosis (SWRO) desalination plant was evaluated using both in-situ fouling monitoring methods and theoretical standardisation and normalisation methods. The results showed that overall performance of the plant deteriorated after 6 months of operation due to fouling. In order to determine the identity and cause of th~ fouling two SWRO membranes were subjected to destructive membrane autopsy. The results showed formation of severe fouling on the surface of both membranes. Microscopic studies using atomic force microscopy (AFM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with Energy Dispersion X-ray spectrometer (EDX), elucidated this layer. AFM, SEM and EDX results showed different types of fouling includes scaling, colloidal and biological fouling. The presence of these foulants on the membrane surfaces indicates malfunctions in the pre-treatment systems used 'in the plant, ultimately resulting in the formation of composite fouling. The effect of this composite fouling on the performance of the RO membrane systems was investigated using a laboratory-scale RO unit and raw seawater samples from the Mediterranean and the North Seas. A rapid flux decline was observed. In order to eliminate the formation of the composite fouling in the RO membrane systems, a novel fouling prevention method was examined. This was a depth ~ filter (DisruptorTM) made of nanoalumina fibres upstream 'to the RO membranes. The results show that this depth filter removes the majority of substances which cause the fouling on the RO membranes. Results are discussed in relation to the practicalities, of desalination plant operation.

system.value: Assessing graphene oxide for water desalination applications

abstract.value: Water desalination plays a critical role in augmenting the fresh water supplies for water scarce regions. However, despite considerable improvements in system efficiencies, it still remains six to ten times more expensive than treating freshwater for drinking. As a result, the construction and operation of a desalination plant places considerable economic burden on the regions that require such an investment. As more and more regions experience water stress due to climate change, increased industrial consumption, and population growth, materials engineering will play a role in improving the economics. The membranes used in today's reverse osmosis plants are made from polymers that are fragile, limited in the flux, and typically operate at 70% of their rated performance due to biofouling. Following the exciting proposition of using graphene as a size-exclusion based desalination membrane, there has been a great deal of revived interest in the development of new membrane materials that overcome these challenges. Graphene oxide, made from the chemical exfoliation of graphite, has served as a promising candidate for membrane applications because it is cheaper than graphene to produce and yet demonstrates similar benefits of resilience and increased permeability. In this work, we take a critical look at three aspects of graphene oxide as it applies to the development of water desalination membranes. First, we present an atomic study of the structure of graphene oxide (GO) that is produced in bulk quantities. In contrast to previous work, which has examined particularly defect free GO, we find that GO develops a nanocrystalline structure in support of a Dynamic Structural Model in its hexagonal carbon lattice. Second, we detail the development of a new cross-linker that enables the fabrication of stable GO films with sub-nanometer interlayer spacing and demonstrated nanofiltration performance. The process of cross-linking and membrane fabrication is entirely solution based and therefore promising for scale up. Finally, we evaluate the techno-economic feasibility of a GO as a water desalination material with a comparison between estimated production cost and savings in terms of the levelized cost of water. We quantitatively assess GO membranes as a scalable technology and identify other separation areas that could be served by robust membrane materials. With these

system.value: Technological challenges of seawater desalination: analysis of future opportunities

abstract.value: This paper deals with an assessment of solar thermal-powered desalination technologies in order to identify key issues for developing market opportunities.The topic of selecting the best solar desalination solution is analysed, case by case, considering different scenes: i) Rural communities with limited fresh water demand; ii) Regions with high demands of both, water and electricity and iii) Intermediate water demands.Detailed analyses of solar thermal-driven desalination -i.e.distillation and Reverse Osmosis (RO) -in comparison to solar PV/RO are presented.The quantitative assessment performed highlights that membrane distillation systems, when fully developed, will have market opportunities at very small-capacity seawater desalination systems.Besides that, dish concentrators coupled to micro gas turbines in case of limited water demand is a promising option.A single unit could produce about 10 m3/h of fresh water from seawater and several units could be coupled to drive the same desalination plant.Moreover, the only stand-alone systems with market opportunities for intermediate water production are based on reverse osmosis driven by parabolic troughs or linear Fresnel concentrators by means of organic Rankine Cycles.Finally, water demands over 25,000 m 3 /d require both, a solar power plant and a reverse osmosis desalination plant.

system.value: Parameters affecting the desalination of seawater reverse osmosis : pre-treatments, membranes processes and environmental impact

abstract.value: Paramètres affectants le dessalement de l'eau de mer par osmose inverse : prétraitement, procédés membranaires et impact environnemental Ce travail a été réalisé dans le cadre d’une étude lancée par la compagnie HUTA sur ses installations de dessalement d’eau de mer. Le procédé de dessalement des eaux de mer le plus utilisé pour la production d’eau douce est l’osmose inverse (SWRO). Une station type, installée dans d’une zone industrielle, a été choisie pour mener cette étude d’optimisation du fonctionnement pour réduire les coûts d’exploitation. L’impact des rejets des rejets sur le milieu naturel a été également étudié. La station de dessalement sélectionnée pour les travaux de recherches est située dans la région Ouest de l’Arabie Saoudite à 160 km au nord de Djeddah, dans une zone industrielle pétrochimique (Raffinerie PETRO RABIGH), site ultra sécurisée, les captages des eaux de mer se font dans la zone côtière proche du site en Mer Rouge.L’étude se concentre principalement sur 3 parties : La première concerne la prise d’eau "INTAKE", différent mode captage ont été testé avec l’installation d’un ouvrage développé spécifiquement pour la station de Rabigh en s’adaptant aux règles imposées par les autorités Saoudienne. La deuxième est réservée aux procédés membranaires et l’importance des prétraitements dans la filière de désalinisation. La dernière partie concerne l’étude d’impact environnemental des rejets industriels "OUTLET" sur le milieu récepteur.

candidates.mechanism: Biofilm fouling is mitigated by introducing a chemically modified nanocellulose layer that disrupts microbial adhesion via surface charge repulsion and reduced organic binding sites (domain knowledge: biofilm adhesion is governed by surface energy and electrostatic interactions; evidence: chemical modification of nanocellulose improves surface affinity and reactivity for contaminant separation).
candidates.intervention: Replace the current polyamide RO membrane with a **hybrid composite membrane** where the selective layer is a chemically modified bacterial nanocellulose (BNC) matrix (thickness: 50–100 nm) embedded with quaternary ammonium groups (QAGs) to impart permanent positive charge, overlaid on a standard thin-film composite (TFC) support. The BNC layer is cross-linked with citric acid to enhance mechanical stability.

evidence_bundle.mechanism_source_span: "The chemical modification of nanocellulose can definitely improve the surface affinity as well as the reactivity of membranes for the efficient separation of specific contaminants/ions."

cemetery_warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
cemetery_warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: Biofilm fouling is mitigated by introducing a chemically modified nanocellulose layer that disrupts microbial adhesion via surface charge repulsion and reduced organic binding sites (domain knowledge: biofilm adhesion is governed by surface energy and electrostatic interactions; evidence: chemical modification of nanocellulose improves surface affinity and reactivity for contaminant separation).
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Replace the current polyamide RO membrane with a **hybrid composite membrane** where the selective layer is a chemically modified bacterial nanocellulose (BNC) matrix (thickness: 50–100 nm) embedded with quaternary ammonium groups (QAGs) to impart permanent positive charge, overlaid on a standard thin-film composite (TFC) support. The BNC layer is cross-linked with citric acid to enhance mechanical stability.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: Fouling is reduced by increasing the membrane’s **hydrodynamic shear resistance** to biofilm accumulation via a nanocellulose-based **spacer modification** in the feed spacers (domain knowledge: biofilm growth is shear-limited in spiral-wound modules; evidence: nanocellulose’s mechanical properties enable structural reinforcement).
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Replace standard polypropylene feed spacers with **bacterial nanocellulose (BNC)-reinforced spacers** (filament diameter: 0.8 mm, porosity: 85%, BNC content: 15% by weight). The BNC is functionalized with polyethylene glycol (PEG, MW 20 kDa) to enhance hydrophilicity and reduce organic fouling. The spacer geometry is optimized to increase cross-flow velocity near the membrane surface by **20%** (via computational fluid dynamics validation).

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: Fouling is suppressed by **dynamic surface regeneration** via a nanocellulose-based **antifouling coating** that releases biocidal agents in response to biofilm formation (domain knowledge: controlled-release coatings can disrupt biofilm matrix integrity; evidence: chemical modification of nanocellulose enhances reactivity for contaminant separation).
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Apply a **cellulose nanocrystal (CNC)-based dynamic coating** (thickness: 20–30 nm) to the polyamide membrane surface, loaded with **silver nanoparticles (AgNPs, 5–10 nm)** at 0.1% w/w. The CNC is cross-linked with genipin to enable pH-triggered release of Ag+ ions (release rate: 0.5–1.0 µg/cm²/day at pH 6–8). The coating is applied via layer-by-layer assembly with polyethylenimine (PEI) for adhesion.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Pre-treatment coverage-aware deployment of ultrafiltration (UF) as a standalone biofilm mitigation layer** — UF reduces organic fouling precursors (biofilm nutrients) in feedwater, extending RO membrane intervals between cleanings by leveraging the same coverage-aware cost-volume tradeoff logic. The mechanism relies on UF’s ability to reject high-molecular-weight organics (>100 kDa) that drive biofilm formation, while the coverage-aware model ensures economic viability by optimizing UF deployment density relative to RO train capacity.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Insert a **hybrid UF-RO configuration** (Configuration A) upstream of the SWRO train, sized to achieve **30–50% coverage of total feedwater** (aligned with the 50% coverage point in the evidence). UF modules are selected for 90%+ rejection of >100 kDa organics (literature-derived parameters) and operated at 50–70 L/m²h flux to minimize fouling.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Dual-stage RO with interstage UF (Configuration B analog)** — A **two-pass RO system** where the first pass (RO1) operates at **lower recovery (30–40%)** to reject >90% of biofilm-forming organics, followed by **UF polishing** of the concentrate (to recover water and further reduce organics), then a second RO pass (RO2) at target recovery. The mechanism exploits the **crossover cost advantage of Configuration B** (>0.98 USD/m³) to justify the added capital, while UF in the interstage mitigates biofilm regrowth by removing residual organics.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Replace the single SWRO train with a **two-stage system**:

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Coverage-optimized UF-RO hybrid with dynamic placement** — **Spatial segmentation of the RO train** into high-fouling and low-fouling zones, where **UF pre-treatment is dynamically allocated** to the high-fouling zones based on real-time fouling sensors (e.g., differential pressure or flux decay). The mechanism leverages the **placement-dominated net-benefit variance** from the evidence to concentrate UF coverage where it maximizes biofilm mitigation, while minimizing capital/operating costs by avoiding full-train UF.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Divide the SWRO train into **4 parallel skids**, each with independent fouling monitoring. Install **modular UF side-streams** (each treating **10–25% of a skid’s feedwater**) that can be **activated/deactivated per skid** based on fouling rate. UF modules are sized for **95% rejection of >10 kDa organics** (literature-derived). Control logic: if a skid’s normalized flux droop exceeds **8% over 7 days**, its UF side-stream is activated for **48 hours**; if droop <3%, UF is deactivated.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: The same **coverage-aware cost-benefit crossover mechanism** as in the source system, where a **dual-stage pretreatment configuration** (e.g., ultrafiltration + alternative non-chlorine biofilm control) shifts the economic and operational break-even point for biofilm mitigation by altering the sensitivity of treatment costs to feed conditions. Domain knowledge: biofilm fouling costs scale with cleaning frequency and chemical dose; the source system’s crossover analysis shows how configuration choice dominates net-benefit variance under adverse feed conditions. Evidence basis: "Adverse feed conditions that couple operating and cost parameters make treatment costs comparably influential for Configuration B" and "placement dominates net-benefit variance."
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Replace the single-stage RO train with a **hybrid pretreatment stage (e.g., ultrafiltration or ceramic microfiltration) paired with a biofilm-resistant RO membrane variant (e.g., high-flux polyamide with embedded antimicrobials or fouling-release coatings)**. The hybrid stage reduces organic/biofilm precursor load, while the membrane variant tolerates longer intervals between CIP. Retain the same permeate recovery by adjusting staging pressure.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: The **placement-dominated net-benefit variance mechanism** from the source system, where **spatial heterogeneity in biofilm accumulation** (analogous to "placement" in the source’s coverage model) enables targeted intervention to reduce system-wide fouling costs. Domain knowledge: biofilm growth is spatially correlated in RO trains (e.g., higher near feed spacers or low-velocity zones); the source system shows placement dominates variance in net benefits. Evidence basis: "placement dominates net-benefit variance" and "approved demand rather than recovery limits volume in at least 98.8% of draws."
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Implement **dynamic flux management** by dividing the RO train into **modular subarrays (each ≤500 m²)** with independent cleaning triggers and variable recovery targets. Use online biofilm sensors (e.g., electrochemical or optical) to detect fouling hotspots and isolate subarrays for targeted CIP or reduced-flux operation. Retain overall permeate recovery by compensating with cleaner subarrays.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: The **configuration-dependent crossover cost mechanism** from the source system, where **switching to a higher-capital but lower-operating-cost configuration** (analogous to Configuration B) alters the fouling cost sensitivity to feed salinity and concentrate disposal. Domain knowledge: biofilm fouling is exacerbated by high salt concentration (osmotic stress promotes microbial adhesion); the source system’s Configuration B (ultrafiltration + RO) shows higher sensitivity to feed salinity. Evidence basis: "Feed salinity... moves the crossover most" and "Configuration B is preferable above a crossover value of 0.98 USD/m³."
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Replace the current RO membrane with a **high-salt-tolerant variant (e.g., thin-film nanocomposite or boron-doped polyamide)** paired with a **low-pressure ultrafiltration (UF) stage operating at 50% of feed flow**. The UF stage removes >90% of biofilm precursors, while the RO variant tolerates higher salinity in the concentrate stream, reducing osmotic fouling drivers. Adjust staging to maintain permeate recovery.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Biofilm growth is driven by organic carbon availability in feedwater; reducing organic carbon concentration via adsorption reduces microbial substrate availability, slowing biofilm formation** (domain knowledge: biofilm growth kinetics depend on organic carbon concentration; standard practice: activated carbon or adsorbent media for organic removal).
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: **Install a dedicated granular activated carbon (GAC) pretreatment stage upstream of the RO feed to adsorb organic carbon and reduce microbial substrate availability**.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Biofilm formation is accelerated by nutrient-rich colloidal particles (e.g., humics, proteins) that adhere to membrane surfaces; hydrodynamic shear stress from optimized feed spacers disrupts particle deposition and biofilm attachment** (domain knowledge: colloidal fouling precedes biofilm formation; standard practice: high-shear spacers to mitigate particle deposition).
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: **Replace standard RO feed spacers with high-shear, turbulence-promoting spacers (e.g., "turbulence-promoting" or "anti-fouling" spacers) to increase wall shear stress and reduce particle/microbe adhesion**.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Biofilm persistence is maintained by extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) produced by microbes; periodic low-concentration non-oxidizing biocides (e.g., peracetic acid or quaternary ammonium compounds) disrupt EPS without damaging polyamide membranes** (domain knowledge: EPS stabilization enables biofilm resilience; standard practice: non-oxidizing biocides for biofilm control in RO systems).
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: **Implement a continuous low-dose non-oxidizing biocide injection (e.g., 0.5–1.0 ppm peracetic acid or 5–10 ppm quaternary ammonium compound) upstream of the RO feed to disrupt EPS and inhibit biofilm growth without membrane damage**.

CROSS_DOMAIN_MIN_NONGENERIC_OVERLAP.justification: R377 patent-text ground truth (TOSCANINI/R377_PATENT_TEXT_FETCH.json + R377_PATENT_TEXT_GROUND_TRUTH.json): 12/30 family representatives (40%) were substantively irrelevant cross-domain term collisions (CWDM optical link for a battery-thermal candidate; dental-condition monitoring for rolling stock; bone fracture forceps for rail steel...). A hit sharing NO entity term with the candidate now needs >= 3 NON-generic mechanism terms to be mechanism art: the measured true cross-domain analog (line-pipe steel with hydrogen fracture toughness for a rail-steel candidate) shares 3 non-generic terms and survives; every measured false positive shares <= 2 and is demoted. This RAISES the cross-domain bar (was the same >= 2 as same-domain) — stricter, not weaker (Art. VII).
CROSS_DOMAIN_MIN_NONGENERIC_OVERLAP.uncertainty: term overlap remains a proxy; entity word-sense collisions ('gear': steering vs draft) can still pass — disclosed limitation, not a solved problem

MIN_MECHANISM_OVERLAP.justification: same term-overlap rule family as the pipeline relevance adjudicator and the Q2 instrument (>= 2 shared content terms = domain-specific rather than accidental collision); NOT weakened relative to any prior gate
MIN_MECHANISM_OVERLAP.uncertainty: term overlap is a proxy for mechanism identity

ANTICIPATION_COVERAGE_RATIO.justification: a family ANTICIPATES only when nearly ALL elements of the candidate's FULL distinguishing set (uncapped — the claim elements, not the 6-term query core) appear in the family's claim/abstract text; 0.8 leaves a >= 20% element margin — anything lower would convert partial art into a kill (Art. XXVIII forbids). Measured adversarial case: a domain-only patent reached 0.857 against a capped denominator whose true differentiators (acoustic, multi-modal) had been ranked out
ANTICIPATION_COVERAGE_RATIO.uncertainty: claim coverage measured by term overlap, not a claim chart; recorded per family with evidence tier

MAX_QUERY_TERMS.justification: provider-measured sweet spot for keyword patent queries (longer queries dilute ranking)

ABSTRACT_TIER_MIN_CHARS.justification: below ~80 chars a snippet carries title echoes, not mechanism description; it cannot support an abstract-tier coverage decision

search_execution.note: status is derived from execution, not findings: a failed/timeout query set can never support a no-match claim (R394 s2/s4, Art. XXI.3)

A single favorable rank calculation under a convenient model is INSUFFICIENT. A single unfavorable perturbation model is ALSO INSUFFICIENT to claim universal non-identifiability — it only kills the specific estimator tested under that specific perturbation model. The correct procedure: (a) define state, observables, inputs, noise, known/unknown params; (b) build measurement equations; (c) test rank of Jacobian wrt unknown params; (d) perform adversarial model-uncertainty test: relax each assumption toward realistic physics and re-test identifiability under the combined relaxed model; (e) only if BOTH the ideal-model rank AND the adversarial-model rank hold (or constructively fail) can a universal claim (measurable OR non-measurable) be recorded.

warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-017: A discovery engine earns trust when it attacks its own successful proof harder than its unsuccessful ideas. Structural identifiability under a convenient model is not enough. A candidate must survive adversarial model uncertainty AND practical operation (safety, timing, decision value, first-pass vs post-hoc). The burden is bidirectional: (a) the proposer must demonstrate identifiability survives realistic model relaxation; (b) the killer must demonstrate non-identifiability holds under EVERY plausible estimator and measurement protocol, not just the one they chose to attack. When in doubt, the implementation is killed; the scientific question stays open until either (a) a survivor is found or (b) an explicit non-identifiability counterexample is constructed (two physically distinct latent states producing indistinguishable observations under ALL measurement protocols).

warnings.territory: Cross-cutting (extracted from Round 62 capability collision failure; applies to ALL novelty claims)
warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM (sharpened per CEO Round 56o): 'Existing information + existing transformation + existing control, merely recombined, is insufficient. A combination qualifies only if it produces a demonstrably new technical effect that survives prior art and non-obviousness attack. A world-class invention needs a genuinely new technical information source, transformation, or control capability. Do not build an AI layer on top of an already-claimed sensing/control architecture.' NOTE: This theorem does NOT create a universal 'new sensor required' rule. A novel combination of existing measurements CAN qualify if it produces a new, technically non-obvious effect. The theorem rejects TRIVIAL recombination, not all combinations.

warnings.lesson: A signal can be GENUINELY ORTHOGONAL to a specific measurement architecture (Hakim measures pressure, not HRV) and still be a DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCE of the same physiological variable (ICP → sympathetic → HRV). Orthogonality to one architecture does not imply independence from the underlying physiology. Before claiming a signal is 'new information,' test whether it is causally downstream of an already-measured variable. If A → B and A is measured, then B is a proxy for A, not new information — even if B is measured by a different sensor.

warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-016 (sharpened per CEO Round 58): A proposed latent quantity survives only when (1) identifiability is demonstrated under an EXPLICIT observation/dynamics model with full rank/observability analysis (not naive unknown-count), AND (2) identifiability REMAINS under plausible model uncertainty (each ideal assumption relaxed toward realistic physics and re-tested). A single favorable rank calculation under a convenient model is INSUFFICIENT. A single unfavorable perturbation model is ALSO INSUFFICIENT to claim universal non-identifiability — it only kills the specific estimator tested under that specific perturbation model. The correct procedure: (a) define state, observables, inputs, noise, known/unknown params; (b) build measurement equations; (c) test rank of Jacobian wrt unknown params; (d) perform adversarial model-uncertainty test: relax each assumption toward realistic physics and re-test identifiability under the combined relaxed model; (e) only if BOTH the ideal-model rank AND the adversarial-model rank hold (or constructively fail) can a universal claim (measurable OR non-measurable) be recorded.

warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-017: A discovery engine earns trust when it attacks its own successful proof harder than its unsuccessful ideas. Structural identifiability under a convenient model is not enough. A candidate must survive adversarial model uncertainty AND practical operation (safety, timing, decision value, first-pass vs post-hoc). The burden is bidirectional: (a) the proposer must demonstrate identifiability survives realistic model relaxation; (b) the killer must demonstrate non-identifiability holds under EVERY plausible estimator and measurement protocol, not just the one they chose to attack. When in doubt, the implementation is killed; the scientific question stays open until either (a) a survivor is found or (b) an explicit non-identifiability counterexample is constructed (two physically distinct latent states producing indistinguishable observations under ALL measurement protocols).

warnings.territory: Cross-cutting (extracted from Round 62 capability collision failure; applies to ALL novelty claims)
warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.
